title: Beyond Model Serving: Running Production LLMs on Kubernetes with KServe
tldr: KServe maintainers explain LLMInferenceService, a separate API from InferenceService that wraps llm-d, vLLM and Gateway API Inference Extension routing so one resource can describe single-node, multi-node and prefill/decode-disaggregated deployments. They then walk through production patterns: cache-aware routing, timeouts, queue-based autoscaling, cold-start reduction, rollouts and LoRA adapters.

key_points.text: LLMs differ from predictive models: they generate tokens over time, hold GPU memory for KV cache, and run long requests, so scheduling, scaling and load balancing need rethinking.
KServe integrates llm-d rather than building an inference engine, and has to keep up with llm-d's fast release pace without bloating its API.

LLMInferenceService has a workload controller (single node, multi-node, separate prefill pool) and a route controller (scheduler and Gateway API resources); it is kept separate so InferenceService stays simple.

One YAML sets model source (Hugging Face, S3, PVC or OCI), tensor/data parallelism, an optional independently scaled prefill pool, and router, gateway and scheduler settings; KServe creates the rest from presets.
The endpoint picker (EPP, the llm-d scheduler) picks a replica using prefix cache match, queue depth and KV cache usage, built on Gateway API Inference Extension; users can plug in a custom EPP.
For streaming, route timeouts must exceed generation time and each hop's timeout must exceed the next one, or clients retry and pile more load on GPUs.

Disaggregated prefill/decode gives consistent TTFT and TPOT at high concurrency and allows different GPU types per phase; very large models use multi-node with LeaderWorkerSet, tensor parallelism within a node and pipeline parallelism across nodes.
Autoscale on the engine's waiting-queue length: GPU utilization reads near 100% with only a few requests because it is a time-share metric, and KV cache utilization sits at a medium baseline.

Cold start: a local model cache, plus container snapshot and restore (CRI-O, NVIDIA Dynamo), cuts startup from tens of minutes to seconds. A shared KV pool keeps TTFT low for new versions during canary rollouts.
Multiple LoRA adapters on one shared base vLLM model are selected per request and save GPU memory.
Q&A: KV cache offloading (LMCache, Dynamo, vLLM connectors) is transparent to KServe; the llm-d router must know where blocks are offloaded to route well.

numbers.text: llm-d went from v0.4 in November 2025 to v1.0 the month before the talk.
Pipeline parallelism example: two nodes with eight GPUs each.
Snapshot/restore cuts cold start from tens of minutes to a few seconds.
Aggregated serving can show P99 at 2-3x baseline versus disaggregated.

open_gaps.text: Next focus is agentic workloads: routing by request type and complexity with llm-d, and SLAs per workload class.
Fast cold start does not solve rollout traffic: new versions have no KV cache unless a shared KV pool is added.
Dashboards hide queueing; end-to-end latency can look flat while TTFT and TPOT degrade.

opportunities.text: Autoscale vLLM replicas in KServe on waiting-queue length instead of GPU utilization.
Audit timeouts from client through load balancer, AI gateway and EPP so each exceeds the one downstream.
Start with aggregated LLMInferenceService, then move to prefill/decode disaggregation, then multi-node LeaderWorkerSet as scale grows.
Help KServe with agentic-workload routing and per-workload SLAs on top of llm-d.
